abstract: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a rare, multi-system genetic disorder characterized by developmental and cognitive impairments with systemic manifestations. Among the genes associated with CdLS, loss-of-function variants in HDAC8 account for approximately 4% of cases (referred to as CdLS5), causing the dysregulation of the cohesin complex, a core pathogenic mechanism of the disorder. Currently, no gene-based therapeutic strategy exists to directly address CdLS resulting from HDAC8 deficiency. Here, we created a new CdLS5 mouse model by introducing a clinically reported HDAC8 p.Ile19Ser variant in the mouse Hdac8 gene using CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Comprehensive molecular, morphological, and behavioral characterization revealed that the new Hdac8I19S mouse strain exhibits a robust phenotype, including marked alterations in deacetylase activity and pronounced developmental and behavioral deficits. This model was subsequently used to evaluate a gene augmentation approach aimed at increasing HDAC8 protein levels and restoring cohesin function through delivery of human HDAC8 transgene. Two AAV vectors driving expression of human HDAC8 were assessed. Although efficient delivery and robust expression were achieved, only modest effects on Smc3 acetylation, a key HDAC8 substrate, were observed, and no significant improvement in cognitive or behavioral phenotypes was detected. Overall, these findings demonstrate that postnatal HDAC8 gene augmentation resulted in limited biochemical correction and minimal phenotypic improvement under the conditions tested. These results highlight important biological considerations, including target engagement and developmental timing, that should be considered in the development of effective therapies for cohesin-related disorders.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acquired resistance to osimertinib mediated by the EGFR C797S mutation remains a major therapeutic challenge in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with limited effective treatment options. This study explored whether abemaciclib, an FDA-approved CDK4/6 inhibitor, can overcome C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
METHODS: A high-throughput screen of approximately 125,000 compounds was performed using Ba/F3 cells expressing EGFR triple mutations (L858R/T790M/C797S and Del19/T790M/C797S). The impact of abemaciclib on EGFR kinase activity was evaluated via in vitro kinase and Western blot assays. Apoptosis induction was assessed using flow cytometry. The activity of abemaciclib was evaluated using biochemical assays, cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA), molecular docking analyses, CRISPR-engineered isogenic models, xenografts, and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models.
RESULTS: Abemaciclib was identified as a potent inhibitor of EGFR triple-mutant cell growth and exhibited preferential activity toward mutant EGFR-dependent models. IL-3 rescue assays demonstrated that its antiproliferative effects were dependent on suppression of oncogenic EGFR signaling. Abemaciclib inhibited mutant EGFR kinase activity, reduced EGFR phosphorylation, and induced apoptotic cell death in osimertinib-resistant models while exhibiting substantially weaker activity toward wild-type EGFR. CETSA and molecular docking analyses supported direct engagement of mutant EGFR by abemaciclib. Importantly, abemaciclib significantly suppressed tumor growth in CRISPR-engineered isogenic xenografts and PDX models harboring EGFR C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance.
CONCLUSIONS: Abemaciclib selectively suppresses C797S-mutant EGFR signaling and demonstrates robust antitumor activity in preclinical models of osimertinib-resistant EGFR-mutant NSCLC. This breakthrough not only overcomes the existing therapeutic barrier but also demonstrates minimal interference with WT EGFR, offering a transformative and precise therapeutic strategy with significant translational and clinical potential. These findings support the therapeutic repurposing of abemaciclib as a potential treatment strategy for EGFR C797S-mediated resistance and provide a translational strategy for overcoming resistance-associated EGFR alterations using clinically available targeted agents.

abstract: Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy increasingly recognised as a cause of heart failure. Advances in the understanding of its pathophysiology have enabled the development of targeted therapies, making ATTR-CM a paradigm of precision medicine in cardiology. Currently approved disease-modifying therapies, including two stabilisers (tafamidis and acoramidis) and one gene-silencing agent (vutrisiran), slow disease progression and reduce hospitalisations and mortality, particularly when initiated early. Because these therapies do not reverse established amyloid deposition, supportive management remains a critical component of care and presents distinct challenges. These include universal anticoagulation in AF, careful diuretic management, the benefits of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and limited tolerance to other foundational heart failure therapies. On-going intensive research is expanding the therapeutic landscape, with several Phase III trials evaluating next-generation silencers, gene-editing strategies and amyloid-removal therapies. While these advances hold promise for disease reversal and prevention, important unresolved issues arise, including optimal treatment selection, monitoring strategies and economic sustainability.

abstract: A new generation of medicines that includes gene therapies, cell-based treatments and gene editors have the potential to treat a vast range of diseases. However, the clinical success of these novel modalities is limited by unwanted immune responses, which can compromise both safety and efficacy. Regulatory agencies have recently emphasized reducing animal testing in preclinical safety studies and envisioned a strategic approach for basing regulatory decisions on scientifically validated new approach methodologies (NAMs). These methods encompass mathematical models, artificial intelligence tools, organ-on-a-chip systems, and advanced in vitro and ex vivo assays. In combination, these approaches seem potentially well suited for assessing unwanted immune responses of the novel modalities. Key challenges to be addressed include predicting the immunogenicity risks from transgene products, delivery vehicles and gene-editing machinery; managing pre-existing immunity; overcoming barriers to repeat dosing; and establishing robust long-term monitoring strategies. In this Perspective, we critically evaluate how the current NAMs toolkit, originally developed for protein therapeutics, can be adapted to assess the unwanted immune responses of novel modalities. We provide a forward-looking framework for developing and validating the next generation of predictive immunogenicity tools required to safely unlock the full therapeutic potential of these revolutionary medicines.

abstract: ADAR1 p150 is an interferon-inducible RNA-editing isoform that limits endogenous double-stranded RNA sensing and can protect tumor cells from inflammatory stress. Yet increased p150 expression has also been observed in immune-infiltrated tumors and in some patients responding to immunotherapy. We argue that elevated p150 abundance is consistent with an interferon-responsive state but cannot, by itself, establish functional ADAR1 dependence or immunotherapy resistance. A practical four-determinant decision framework distinguishes an interferon-exposure interpretation from a tumor-dependency interpretation by examining signaling context, cellular source and localization, treatment timing, and RNA-sensing function. Crucially, editing-independent competition for dsRNA binding can suppress PKR, making RNA-editing measurements insufficient as a sole functional assay. We specify clinically accessible measurements, the limitations of bulk assays, and functional studies required to validate the proposed decision rules. This framework offers testable hypotheses rather than a clinically validated classification system.

abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.

abstract:
RATIONALE: Pulmonary ionocytes, representing approximately 1% of airway epithelial cells, exhibit high CFTR expression and unique transcriptional markers, including FOXI1, ASCL3, and V-ATPase. Their exact role in human airway physiology is incompletely understood.
OBJECTIVE: This study employs induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived airway epithelial models (iPSC-airways) to elucidate the role of FOXI1 in pulmonary ionocyte differentiation and function.
METHODS: CRISPR-Cas9 was used to generate FOXI1-knockout iPSCs, into which a doxycycline-inducible FOXI1-overexpression cassette was introduced. Edited and control lines were differentiated into airway epithelia to evaluate ionocyte formation, epithelial composition, and ion transport. Rescue studies assessed the effects of FOXI1 re-expression in a FOXI1-KO background, and the addition of inducible WT-CFTR ionocytes to F508del/F508del cystic fibrosis (CF) cultures on restoring chloride transport.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: FOXI1 deletion abolishes ionocyte formation and alters airway epithelial composition, with increased mucus-secreting goblet cells and decreased ciliated cells. Functional assays confirmed ionocytes as key regulators of chloride homeostasis, with FOXI1-deficient airways displaying diminished ion transport. Induction of FOXI1-overexpression restored CFTR-mediated chloride transport. Introduction of WT ionocytes into CF airway models rescued chloride transport deficits, with no rescue observed in vehicle-treated controls lacking ionocyte induction.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings highlight FOXI1's essential role in pulmonary ionocyte development, airway cell composition, and airway chloride transport. We present a fully manipulable, gene-edited iPSC-derived system that enables investigation of ionocyte biology and function within a human airway context, highlighting them as promising therapeutic targets for respiratory disorders.

abstract: Oral biofilms are spatially ordered microbial communities whose pathogenic behavior is shaped by more than taxonomic composition. Their development reflects the combined effects of adhesin-receptor recognition, interspecies coaggregation, matrix formation, metabolite exchange, local physicochemical gradients and host-derived selection. Here, we synthesize molecular and ecological evidence on the bacterial cell surface-matrix interface and consider how these interactions contribute to cariogenic, periodontal and peri-implant biofilms. Particular attention is given to glucosyltransferase-dependent polysaccharides, extracellular DNA, amyloidogenic proteins, sortase-anchored surface factors and outer membrane vesicles, together with metabolic interactions involving lactate, arginine, hydrogen peroxide and heme. We further evaluate functional-genomic and systems-level approaches (including transposon sequencing, CRISPR interference, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics, spatial imaging, genome-scale metabolic modeling and machine learning) while distinguishing association and prediction from experimentally demonstrated mechanism. Emerging interventions are assessed according to their biological target and evidence level, including adhesion blockade, specifically targeted antimicrobials, matrix synthesis inhibition and degradation, quorum interference, probiotics, catalytic nanoparticles, antimicrobial photodynamic therapy and antibiofilm dental materials. Across these approaches, reduction in biofilm biomass is not equivalent to ecological restoration or clinical benefit. Key translational barriers include model fidelity, donor-to-donor variation, spatial heterogeneity, treatment durability, endpoint selection and the limited external validation of many computational and preclinical findings. Future precision strategies should therefore integrate microbial identity, matrix architecture, spatial metabolism and host context, with experimental perturbation used to establish causal vulnerabilities before therapeutic translation.

abstract: The transcription factor (TF) SPI1 (historically called PU.1) is a critical pioneer TF and regulator of hematopoiesis. It exerts exquisitely dose-dependent and stage-specific control over lymphoid, myeloid, and central nervous system-resident lineages. Structurally characterized by an intrinsically disordered N-terminal transactivation region and a highly conserved C-terminal DNA-binding E26 transformation-specific domain, SPI1 can operate alone as a monomer, via homodimerization, through epigenetic interactions, and in context-dependent transcriptional partnerships. While early animal models established its essentiality for leukopoiesis, modern human genomics has unveiled direct links between altered SPI1 function and disease. Heterozygous loss-of-function germline variants cause PU.1-mediated agammaglobulinemia, whereas somatic mutations and/or regulatory alterations can drive hematologic malignancies. Dysregulated SPI1 activity is also implicated in autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, and neurodegenerative disorders. This review reconciles foundational murine paradigms with emerging human translational data, highlights current therapeutic landscapes, and projects how single-cell multi-omics and advanced gene editing may shape future directions in the SPI1 biomedical field.

abstract: Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) at an early stage of transcription initiation. Fidaxomicin is used for treating Clostridioides difficile infections and has demonstrated in vitro efficacy against drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). Fidaxomicin derivatives are currently the focus of extensive research to develop novel antibacterial agents. Previous studies showed that region 3.2 of the RNAP primary σ factor and the mycobacterial transcriptional activator RbpA modulate fidaxomicin potency through poorly understood mechanisms. Moreover, the impact of the structurally distinct extracytoplasmic function (ECF) σ factors on fidaxomicin potency has never been explored. Here, using DNA scaffold-based in vitro transcription assays, we found that RbpA-dependent primary σ factors from Mtb enhance fidaxomicin potency, whereas ECF σ factors render Mtb RNAP resistant to fidaxomicin. Contrary to the prevailing assumptions, RbpA has only a marginal effect on fidaxomicin potency. Our structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations support a model in which ECF σ factors obstruct fidaxomicin binding by changing the configuration of the RNAP RNA channel. Conversely, the direct interaction between fidaxomicin and RbpA-dependent primary σ factors does not affect drug binding. Our findings identify the σ factor as a key modulator of fidaxomicin potency and provide a framework to explore σ factor structural diversity for designing pathogen-specific fidaxomicin analogs. Moreover, these results highlight fundamental mechanistic differences between the modes of action of housekeeping and ECF σ factors during transcription initiation.

abstract: Buffaloes are important contributors to agricultural production in many developing countries, yet poor semen cryosurvival remains a major challenge for efficient artificial insemination and genetic improvement. In recent years, small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) have emerged as important mediators of intercellular communication and reproductive function; however, their potential as supplements for improving buffalo semen cryosurvival remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study evaluated the influence of adding a seminal plasma-derived small extracellular vesicle-enriched preparation to a Tris extender using post-thaw sperm traits, oxidative status, DNA integrity, HSP70 and PRM1 transcript abundance, and fertility of Kundhi buffalo bull semen. Seminal plasma-derived particles were isolated and characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis, showing a mean diameter of 117.8 ± 2.47 nm, modal diameter of 89.4 ± 1.41 nm, and concentration of (3.21 ± 0.05) × 1011 particles/mL. Thirty-two ejaculates from four Kundhi buffalo bulls were pooled and extended with a Tris extender supplemented with 0, 25, 50, 100, or 200 μg/mL sEV-enriched preparation before cryopreservation. Post-thaw sperm quality, early apoptosis, DNA fragmentation, lipid peroxidation, antioxidant enzymes, and relative mRNA abundance of HSP70 and PRM1 were assessed. All evaluated post-thaw variables differed (P < 0.05) after supplementation, whereas 50 μg/mL revealed the strongest response. The EV-50 group showed higher total motility, progressive motility, viability, and HOST-positive spermatozoa, however reduced early apoptotic sperm, DNA fragmentation, and MDA concentration than the control group. EV-50 also enhanced SOD, catalase, total glutathione, HSP70 and PRM1 expression (1.91 ± 0.07-fold and 1.69 ± 0.05-fold, respectively). In fertility validation, pregnancy rate increased from 41.7% in the control group to 56.7% in the EV-50-treated semen group, with higher odds of pregnancy (OR = 1.83; P = 0.028). In conclusion, supplementation with 50 μg/mL of the sEV-enriched preparation improved post-thaw sperm quality, redox homeostasis, DNA integrity, HSP70 and PRM1 transcript abundance, and field fertility, supporting its potential as a cryopreservation supplement for enhancing the reproductive performance of Kundhi buffalo semen.

abstract: Post-transcriptional RNA modifications have emerged as a crucial layer of epigenetic regulation in eukaryotes, profoundly influencing mRNA processing, stability, and translational efficiency. As RNA modification research expands from mammalian systems to plants, its significance for crop improvement and environmental adaptation is becoming increasingly evident. This review synthesizes current research on the plant epitranscriptomic landscape-primarily focusing on N6-methyladenosine (m6A), alongside N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C), 5-methylcytosine (m5C), 1-methyladenosine (m1A), 7-methylguanosine (m7G), and pseudouridine (Ψ). By exploring the dynamic machinery of specific "writers," "erasers," and "readers," we highlight how these epitranscriptomic marks orchestrate plant growth, developmental phase transitions, and adaptive responses to abiotic stresses in model species and major crops. Rapid advances in detection methods, from conventional chromatography to third-generation single-molecule sequencing, have largely driven these biological insights. Although regulatory mechanisms and cross-species conservation of most modifications beyond m6A remain poorly understood, their translational potential is undeniable. Ultimately, we discuss how leveraging gene-editing technologies to manipulate these epitranscriptomic pathways offers a transformative strategy for molecular breeding, aiming to enhance crop yield, nutritional quality, and abiotic stress tolerance.

abstract: In this edition, we highlight several important developments across the Huntington's disease therapeutic pipeline. We discuss the launch and subsequent discontinuation of POINT-HD, the first-in-human phase I study of RG6496 (Hoffmann-La Roche), an allele-selective antisense oligonucleotide designed to selectively lower mutant huntingtin while largely preserving wild-type huntingtin expression. We also discuss the launch of two phase III efficacy trials: INVEST-HD, evaluating votoplam (Novartis Pharmaceuticals), and PRECISE-HD, evaluating pridopidine (Prilenia). In addition, we summarise recent advances across the field, including preclinical updates for LQT-23 (LoQus23), SRP-1005 (Sarepta Therapeutics) and HRN001 (Harness Therapeutics); interim 12-month clinical results from SKY-0515 (Skyhawk Therapeutics); the announcement by uniQure that 3-year data from the phase I/II AMT-130 study may support a Biologics License Application seeking accelerated approval and Roche's discontinuation of the phase II GENERATION HD2 study of tominersen. Finally, we provide an updated listing of registered and ongoing clinical trials in Huntington's disease.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, yet current therapeutic strategies lack sustained efficacy and long-term stability. Our study aimed to construct a humanized rodent model for drugs development especially currently prevalent small interfering RNA medication.
METHODS: A humanized hypertensive mouse model was generated by subcutaneous injection of neonatal mice with adeno-associated viruses encoding hAGT (human angiotensinogen) and hRENIN (human renin). Blood pressure was monitored weekly via tail-cuff plethysmography. Expression of hAGT and hRENIN was assessed by ELISA, Western blot, and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Cardiac function was evaluated by echocardiography at 4 and 6 months postinjection. Hypertension-associated comorbidities were examined through histological analysis and ELISA. A modified N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA targeting human hepatic AGT (GalNAc-siAGT) was screened and subcutaneously administered to humanized hypertensive mice, either alone or in combination with valsartan, to evaluate therapeutic efficacy.
RESULTS: The dual adeno-associated virus-induced humanized hypertensive model exhibited a sustained hypertension for 6 months and manifested prevalent comorbidities, including heart failure and kidney disease. This modified GalNAc-siAGT demonstrated significant activity in knocking down hAGT both in vitro and in vivo. Only a single subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siAGT in humanized hypertensive mice led to a sustained reduction in blood pressure lasting for 2 months, accompanied by cardio- and renoprotective effects. Moreover, combining GalNAc-siAGT with the renin-angiotensin system blocker, valsartan, significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study validated the antihypertensive therapeutic effect of GalNAc-siAGT in a humanized hypertensive murine model while highlighting the translational potential of this model for clinical drug development.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas genome editing represents one of the most transformative advances in modern molecular biology, enabling programmable site-specific genetic modification that has revolutionized functional genomics and precision therapeutic development. Beyond canonical Cas9 nucleases, the CRISPR toolkit has diversified into precision base editors, prime editors, CRISPR-associated transposases, and Cas12/Cas13 RNA-targeting effectors, each with distinct mechanistic properties. Clinically, ex vivo CRISPR therapies for hemoglobinopathies have secured regulatory approval, while base editing, prime editing, and in vivo Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T candidates are advancing through trials for a broad spectrum of hematologic, oncologic, and rare genetic disorders. However, existing reviews largely address technical innovation or clinical translation in isolation, lacking a holistic, up-to-date synthesis of the full bench-to-bedside trajectory of CRISPR technology. This review systematically dissects the molecular mechanisms, advantages, and limitations of core CRISPR editing platforms; summarizes pivotal clinical data across hemoglobinopathies, CAR-T immunotherapy, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cardiometabolic diseases and rare monogenic diseases; evaluates delivery systems including lipid nanoparticles and viral vectors; and discusses key translational barriers such as off-target genotoxicity and immunogenicity alongside emerging optimization strategies. This work provides a holistic bench-to-bedside framework for CRISPR research, offering critical insights to advance next-generation precision genetic medicine.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Impaired fracture healing remains a significant clinical challenge. Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) and the exosomes (BMSC-Exos) play a pivotal role in bone regeneration, partly by transferring functional microRNAs (miRNAs). A-to-I RNA editing can profoundly alter miRNA function, but its role in fracture healing, particularly for miRNA-99a-5p, is underexplored. We first profiled differentially edited miRNAs in serum from 50 fracture patients and healthy controls. A murine fracture model was established and treated with BMSC-Exos, where either the edited or wild-type form of miRNA-99a-5p was knocked down. In vitro studies involved transfecting BMSCs with ADAR expression vectors to investigate editing mechanisms, and overexpressing/inhibiting edited/wild-type miRNA-99a-5p in MC3T3-E1C osteoblasts to elucidate its direct functional impacts on osteogenic differentiation, apoptosis, proliferation, and migration. Validation of target genes were performed by dual-luciferase reporter assays, qPCR, and Western blot. Key readouts included alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining, flow cytometry, Transwell migration, CCK-8 proliferation assays and HE staining. Clinical analysis revealed significantly lower A-to-I edited miRNA-99a-5p levels in fracture patients, correlating with delayed union. In mice, BMSC-Exos promoted fracture healing, an effect attenuated by edited miRNA-99a-5p knockdown. In vitro, edited miRNA-99a-5p enhanced osteogenesis and inhibited apoptosis, while the wild-type form had opposing effects. ADAR2 mediated this editing. Edited miRNA-99a-5p directly targeted and suppressed Growth Differentiation Factor 11 (GDF11) expression. Importantly, GDF11 overexpression reversed the pro-osteogenic effects of edited miRNA-99a-5p, in both direct and exosome-mediated contexts. Reduced A-to-I editing of miRNA-99a-5p is associated with impaired fracture healing. BMSC-Exos facilitate bone repair by delivering ADAR2-edited miRNA-99a-5p, which promotes osteogenic differentiation and bone formation through the specific targeting and downregulation of GDF11. This study uncovers a novel exosome-mediated RNA editing pathway critical for fracture healing and highlights edited miRNA-99a-5p and GDF11 as potential therapeutic targets for bone repair.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10616-026-01080-x.

abstract: Frailty, an age-related state of increased vulnerability, is associated with greater susceptibility to infection and impaired vaccine response. In this Review, we examine how frailty-associated immunosenescence, including altered haematopoiesis, chronic inflammation, and dysfunction of innate and adaptive immune responses, can affect the immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety of lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines. Evidence from COVID-19 lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines and other vaccines suggests that people living with frailty can mount weaker or less durable responses than non-frail peers, although findings remain heterogeneous and frailty-specific evidence is scarce. The high customisability of lipid nanoparticle mRNA platforms creates opportunities for frailty-tailored vaccination. We discuss optimisation of lipid nanoparticle composition, targeting and dosing, mRNA cargo and combination-vaccine approaches, alongside host-directed measures addressing comorbidities, nutrition, and immune dysfunction. Integrating frailty into vaccine design, evaluation, and deployment could support safer, more effective, and more individualised vaccination strategies for older adults.

title: Frailty as a determinant of mRNA vaccine efficacy.

abstract: Advanced therapeutics, including programmable nucleic acid-based therapies (NATs), such as small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), CRISPR-Cas 9 editing systems, modified in vitro transcribed messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), have the potential to transform healthcare. However, while there have been considerable successes, there have also been notable clinical failures in early-stage human trials, which slowed down the progression of these therapeutic platforms. Multiple trials of NATs have been halted or discontinued, or approved products carry black box warnings as unforeseen or underestimated toxicities and poor efficacy have been observed in humans. There are a variety of reasons for failure of NATs, one of which is that many preclinical studies lack disease modelling in a human-relevant manner and, therefore, do not capture disease-specific effects on therapy tolerability and efficacy. This Perspective provides a short overview of why better human disease modelling is required to understand the potential therapeutic liabilities of NATs across modalities.

abstract: Gynecological cancers, including ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, remain major contributors to female morbidity and mortality worldwide. Conventional treatments-surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy-have improved outcomes, but advanced or recurrent disease is still associated with poor prognosis, chemoresistance, and tumor heterogeneity. Immunotherapy has emerged as a transformative strategy because of its specificity and potential for durable responses. However, the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and inefficient delivery of immunotherapeutic agents limit clinical benefit. Nanocarriers, including organic, inorganic, and biomimetic platforms, can improve targeted delivery, sustained release, biocompatibility, and tumor microenvironment remodeling, thereby enhancing immunotherapy. This review summarizes major immunotherapeutic modalities for gynecological cancers-immune checkpoint blockade, CAR-T cell therapy, tumor vaccines, and oncolytic viruses-and the classification and characteristics of commonly used nanocarriers. We focus on nanocarrier-mediated immunotherapeutic mechanisms in ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, and further highlight emerging lipid nanoparticle/mRNA and programmable RNA delivery strategies. Finally, we analyze challenges in clinical translation and provide perspectives for future development, aiming to support fundamental research and clinical application of nano-immunotherapy in gynecological malignancies.

abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared mechanism across neurological disease. Specifically, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial DNA damage are factors in primary mitochondrial disorders and major neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson, Alzheimer, and Huntington diseases, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This review surveys the mechanisms driving mitochondrial dysfunction and evaluates the current landscape of gene-editing technologies developed to address them. We examine mitochondria-targeted editors and nuclear-targeted editors, examining the editing capability, delivery constraints, and off-target risk of each. Heteroplasmy-shifting nucleases currently offer the strongest in vivo evidence for mtDNA-directed therapy, while base editors extend correction to homoplasmic mutations at the cost of a narrower editing scope and off-target editing. Nuclear editing platforms avoid the mitochondrial gRNA import barrier entirely, allowing current technologies to achieve the most progress toward functional, behavioral rescue in animal models. Across all platforms, delivery efficiency, off-target specificity, and translation from rodent to primate models remain unresolved barriers to clinical application. Gene editing for mitochondrial dysfunction is highly creditable as a precision therapy for genetically defined disease subsets, including primary mitochondrial disease and other neurodegenerative disorders with a known nuclear driver, rather than as a universal strategy for sporadic neurodegeneration, where mitochondrial dysfunction arises from multifactorial and poorly localized causes.

abstract: Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy, and effective gene therapy remains limited by ocular barriers, tumor heterogeneity, and inefficient nucleic acid delivery. This review critically analyses the molecular rationale, engineering principles, emerging nanoarchitectures, biological validation, and translational prospects of dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma. The manuscript also highlights key challenges and future strategies for clinical implementation. Current evidence indicates that dual-vector platforms enable independent optimization of mRNA and CRISPR cargos while maintaining coordinated spatiotemporal therapeutic activity. We conducted a literature search in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for relevant studies published from January 2015 to September 2026. Functional cargo partitioning, vector modularity, programmable intracellular trafficking, and ocular-targeted nanoengineering improve delivery precision and reduce biological compromise associated with co-encapsulation. Lipid, polymeric, hybrid, biomimetic, and viral-nonviral architectures each provide distinct engineering advantages depending on therapeutic objectives. Preclinical studies support enhanced genome editing, transient protein restoration, improved tumor suppression, and reduced off-target effects. Nevertheless, manufacturing scalability, regulatory standardization, long-term safety, and clinical validation remain major barriers to translation. Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR systems represent a promising next-generation platform for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma by enabling coordinated and programmable therapeutic delivery. Continued advances in modular nanoengineering, personalized cargo selection, and clinically scalable manufacturing will be essential for successful translation into precision ocular oncology.

abstract: Viral diseases remain a major global health challenge despite substantial advances in vaccination, antiviral therapeutics, and public-health interventions. However, current antiviral strategies are still constrained by important gaps, including rapid viral evolution, limited broad-spectrum efficacy, immune escape, antiviral resistance, incomplete durability of protection, and inequitable global access to prevention and treatment. This review provides a comprehensive and integrated overview of contemporary antiviral prevention and therapeutic strategies, spanning vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, direct-acting antivirals, host-targeted therapies, immunomodulators, RNA-based therapeutics, gene-editing technologies, and cellular immunotherapies. We discuss the mechanistic foundations, clinical applications, pharmacologic considerations, and translational challenges associated with each modality across major human viral pathogens, including HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, Ebola virus, arboviruses, and herpesviruses. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging innovations such as long-acting prophylaxis, Fc-engineered monoclonal antibodies, nanoparticle and mucosal vaccine platforms, CRISPR-based antiviral systems, and broadly protective host-directed approaches designed to overcome resistance and enhance pandemic preparedness. In addition, we highlight the growing importance of real-time genomic surveillance and equitable global deployment strategies in shaping future antiviral responses, collectively underscoring that the next generation of antiviral medicine will depend on the convergence of universal immunization strategies, durable therapeutics, precision immune modulation, and rapidly deployable platform technologies capable of addressing both endemic and emerging viral threats.

title: Therapeutic and Prophylactic Agents for Viral Diseases: Current Status, Challenges, and Future Prospects.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype characterized by high metastatic potential and limited targeted therapeutic options. Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) has been implicated in tumor progression and metastatic dissemination, but its functional role in TNBC remains incompletely understood. This study investigated the role of LCN2 in the human TNBC cell line MDA-MB-231.
METHODS: Stable LCN2-deficient (LCN2KO) cells were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, followed by isolation of single-cell-derived clones. RNA sequencing was performed to characterize transcriptomic changes, with selected findings validated by reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Western blotting was used to assess protein-level changes. Transwell migration and invasion assays and adhesion assays were performed to evaluate functional effects.
RESULTS: LCN2KO cells largely retained the mesenchymal phenotype of parental cells. RNA sequencing revealed changes associated with inflammatory signaling, iron homeostasis, oxidative stress, ferroptosis-related processes, and cellular metabolism. Functional assays demonstrated reduced migration, invasion, and adhesion, accompanied by altered adhesion to extracellular matrix components.
DISCUSSION: LCN2 deficiency is associated with transcriptional and functional changes in MDA-MB-231 cells, particularly affecting migratory and invasive behavior and cell-matrix interactions, while largely preserving the mesenchymal phenotype. These findings provide further insight into the role of LCN2 in cellular processes relevant to TNBC progression and metastatic behavior.

title: Comprehensive characterization of the cellular and molecular consequences of LCN2 loss in MDA-MB-231 triple-negative breast cancer cells.

abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Conventional modalities, namely surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy, continue to face substantial limitations. The advent of gene therapy, particularly CRISPR-based genome editing, offers new opportunities to overcome these barriers. Nuclease systems such as CRISPR/Cas9 enable precise excision of mutant alleles and targeted insertion of exogenous sequences by harnessing endogenous DNA-repair pathways, achieving durable and accurate genomic modification; derivative tools including CRISPRi, base editing, and prime editing enable diverse forms of gene regulation or precise genome modification through transcriptional repression, base conversion, or related editing mechanisms. To enhance the efficiency, specificity, and spatiotemporal control of CRISPR editing in vivo, sophisticated delivery platforms have been engineered to respond to endogenous tumor-microenvironment cues (e.g., pH, redox potential, hypoxia, ATP, enzymes and microRNAs) or exogenous triggers (e.g., light, ultrasound and magnetic fields). Distinct from material-centric classification schemes, this review organizes these stimuli-responsive systems according to their pathological relevance to the tumor microenvironment (TME), establishing a conceptual framework that links specific TME aberrations with corresponding delivery paradigms. These stimuli-responsive systems represent a major innovation and markedly expand the therapeutic potential of genome editing in oncology. In this review, we summarize the mechanistic basis of CRISPR-based editing, delineate design principles and engineering strategies for stimuli-responsive delivery, and highlight recent advances, outstanding challenges, and future directions toward clinical translation. We aim to provide a concise reference to guide the rational design of gene-editing cancer therapeutics.

title: Stimuli-responsive CRISPR-based genome editing delivery system for cancer treatment: A review of fundamentals and applications.

abstract: Breast cancer progression is driven by molecular heterogeneity, drug resistance (DR), and interactions within the tumour microenvironment (TME), creating an urgent need for therapies that can selectively suppress disease-associated genes. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) can silence targets involved in tumour growth, treatment resistance, and immune evasion. Its therapeutic potential, however, depends on overcoming rapid degradation and clearance, limited tumour accumulation, poor cellular uptake, and endosomal entrapment. Lipid-based and polymer-mediated delivery systems (DS) protect siRNA and facilitate its transport, while chemical modifications, molecular conjugates, and physical delivery methods offer additional ways to improve stability or access to target cells. In BC models, these strategies have been investigated for targeted therapy, reversal of DR, and modulation of the TME to support antitumor immunity. Despite encouraging preclinical findings, effective tumour delivery, sustained gene silencing, off-target effects, and immune activation remain significant barriers to clinical translation. This review brings together advances in siRNA delivery and their applications against BC progression, DR, and immune evasion, while defining the barriers that must be overcome to translate effective gene silencing into meaningful clinical benefit.

abstract:
This is an open-label, single-arm, single-site Phase I trial in a total of 20 healthy participants at GARM Próspera, Roatán, Honduras. Each participant receives one intravenous administration of 0.5 mg AKL003 on Day 0.

Screening is followed by one treatment visit at GARM Próspera covering Day -1 to Day 2. Scheduled follow-up comprises Day 7 and the actual remote Final Visit (nominal Day 28 ±7 days), following local assessments under Investigator oversight.

Safety is assessed through adverse events, clinical examinations, vital signs, ECG and laboratory testing. Six months of passive safety follow-up after the individual Final Visit or Early Termination Visit.

PsyTool, QoL, Oura and DNA methylation assessments are retained. Exploratory changes do not establish clinical efficacy without a concurrent control group.
description:
This is an open-label, single-arm, single-site Phase I trial evaluating safety, tolerability and serum alpha-Klotho protein expression after a single intravenous administration of AKL003, a proprietary alpha-Klotho mRNA formulated in lipid nanoparticles. Twenty participants in total will receive AKL003 at GARM Próspera, Roatán, Honduras.

Each participant will receive one 0.5 mg intravenous administration on Day 0. Screening and later laboratory follow-up may be conducted through designated providers in the USA under the responsible Investigator's oversight. One treatment visit at GARM Próspera, Roatán, Honduras is required, covering Day -1 through Day 2. Scheduled follow-up comprises Day 7 and the actual remote Final Visit (nominal Day 28 ±7 days), following local laboratory and physical assessments. All participants follow the protocol-defined eligibility criteria, dose, pre- and post-treatment dexamethasone regimen, assessment schedule and safety procedures.

Systemic reactogenicity events, including fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea and increased heart rate, will be assessed as adverse events. Severity will be graded ; CRS will be graded according to ASTCT criteria where applicable.

All participants will be informed about potential clinical activity and reactogenicity, which may be influenced by increased aKL serum levels or the lipid nanoparticle formulation. Participants will be instructed to contact the trial site to schedule an on-site visit in case of any unexpected adverse event (unscheduled visit,). All such occurrences will be documented as part of the drug candidate's safety evaluation.

Participants will use an electronic diary for daily symptoms through Day 7 and report new or worsening symptoms promptly throughout follow-up. Quality-of-life questionnaires will be completed at baseline and weekly during follow-up, including the actual Final Visit. Oura-derived measures will be collected from screening through the actual Final Visit. PsyTool assessments and other exploratory measures will be collected at different timepoints.

After the individual Final Visit or Early Termination Visit, safety information received during six months of passive follow-up will be assessed. This period adds no scheduled study visits, routine diary entries, questionnaires or biomarker samples. The Investigator may arrange additional care or assessments when clinically indicated.

The primary purpose is safety and tolerability assessment. Without a concurrent control group, exploratory changes may reflect natural variability, practice effects, concomitant factors or expectation effects. They will be interpreted as hypothesis-generating observations.

abstract: The clinical translation of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics is constrained by limited stability of liquid formulations, necessitating ultra-cold storage and restricting global accessibility. Here, we report a spray-dried dry powder platform for mRNA-LNPs that overcomes these limitations while enabling flexible routes of administration. Systematic evaluation of pharmaceutically relevant sugars identifies trehalose as an optimal matrix former, yielding high-recovery mRNA-LNP dry powder product (DPP) with controlled particle size, low residual moisture, and preserved LNP physicochemical properties upon reconstitution. Mechanistic studies combining solid-state characterization, fluorescence tracking, and solvent extraction demonstrate that mRNA-LNPs are entrapped within an amorphous trehalose matrix core, providing protection against dehydration and rehydration stress. Reconstituted DPP (RDPP) maintains in vivo protein expression comparable to liquid control (LC) following intravenous and intramuscular administration, while supporting effective mucosal delivery via pulmonary and sublingual routes. Direct administration of DPP without reconstitution enables lung-targeted protein expression, highlighting potential for cold-chain-independent therapies. Critically, DPP preserves colloidal stability, mRNA integrity, ionizable lipid stability, and biological activity for over 3 years under refrigerated conditions, whereas liquid formulation exhibits substantial degradation within 6-9 months. These findings establish spray-dried mRNA-LNP DPPs as a robust platform integrating long-term stability with multi-route delivery for improved accessibility of mRNA therapeutics.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Oligonucleotide drug product manufacturing commonly relies on time-consuming offline ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analyses to confirm active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) concentration during mixing, providing limited process visibility. This study evaluated inline Raman spectroscopy as a process analytical technology (PAT) tool for real-time API concentration monitoring and mixing endpoint determination during manufacture of a model antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) drug product.
METHODS: A partial least squares regression (PLSR) model was developed from inline Raman spectra using offline UV-Vis reference concentrations. Accuracy, linearity, range, precision, specificity, and robustness were evaluated, including effects of stirring speed, probe depth, and reusable versus single-use Raman optics. The validated model was applied to four ASO drug product batches manufactured in a 50-L single-use mixer.
RESULTS: The PLSR model demonstrated good accuracy (RMSEP = 3.47 mg/mL), good linearity (R2 = 0.994 and 0.996 for calibration and independent prediction set, respectively), and precision (maximum %RSD = 1.12%). Minimal water interference supported specificity, and consistent performance across stirring speeds, probe depths, and Raman optic configurations demonstrated robustness. The procedure generated real-time ASO API concentration profiles and successfully determined the mixing endpoint for all four batches.
CONCLUSIONS: Inline Raman spectroscopy coupled with PLSR provided accurate, specific, and robust real-time API concentration monitoring during oligonucleotide drug product manufacturing. The approach enabled real-time monitoring and objective mixing endpoint determination and may reduce reliance on offline measurements while improving process visibility and supporting more timely progression of manufacturing operations.

abstract: Efficient engineering of human and murine primary T cells without perturbation of cellular function is crucial for immunotherapy and immunology research. Here, we present a protocol for genome editing of primary T cells with minimal toxicity using peptide-assisted genome editing. We describe key steps required for primary T cell isolation and activation, CRISPR ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assembly and delivery mediated by peptide, and assessment of editing efficiency. This protocol maintains T cell proliferative capacity and functional potency. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Zhang et al.1.

title: Protocol for engineering primary human and mouse T cells using peptide-assisted genome editing.

abstract: R2 retroelements are non-long-terminal-repeat retrotransposons that primarily insert into 28S ribosomal DNA loci across diverse eukaryotes. R2 elements home to their target sites through target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT), in which the R2 protein recognizes and nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription using an R2-encoding RNA as the template. The avian R2 system from Taeniopygia guttata (R2Tg) can insert a payload sequence within an RNA template into 28S ribosomal DNA loci in human cells. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the R2Tg-template RNA-target DNA complex in the TPRT initiation state, both alone and bound to a Cas9-guide RNA complex. These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

title: Structural mechanism of programmable gene integration by the R2 retrotransposon coupled with CRISPR-Cas9.

abstract: The growing resistance to antibiotics by Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a global health threat. Traditional antibiotics act on the viability of bacteria, whereas new ones are now increasingly targeting virulence factors. Phenol-soluble modulins (PSMs) are essential virulence factors that play important roles in inflammation, neutrophil lysis, cytotoxicity and biofilm formation. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar were used for literature search of articles published between 2010 and 2026. Green-synthesized metal nanoparticles (NPs) have been found to be capable of altering these mechanisms by inducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, membrane damage, and by interfering with the quorum-sensing mechanism of the bacteria, along with inhibiting the Agr system. Optimization of NP-based interventions can be supported by multi-omics approaches such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics. Other potential methods of targeted PSM pathway and Agr pathway suppression are also available, such as CRISPR-Cas9 and dCas9, but there are delivery difficulties. The potential use of combining nanotechnology, gene editing, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology could allow for development of more advanced anti-virulence strategies against S. aureus infections targeted at PSM.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines are next-generation platforms capable of eliciting potent cellular and humoral immunity through intracellular expression of tumor-associated or mutation-specific antigens. Canine mammary gland tumor (CMT), commonly encountered in female dogs, frequently harbors mutations in the BRCA2 and p53 genes, which are also relevant to human breast cancers. We aimed to design mutation-targeted mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines encoding canine BRCA2 and p53 variants using in silico epitope prediction and evaluate their immunogenicity and safety. Three mRNA constructs encoding BRCA2 and p53 mutations were synthesized and encapsulated in ionizable-lipid-based LNPs. The resulting mRNA-LNP formulations, namely canine BRCA2-10204ins candidates (cBR2-Cand), canine BRCA2-p53 28-mer epitopes (cBR2-p53), and canine BRCA2-partial (cBR2-Part), were then admixed to prepare the cBR2-cocktail, a mixed mRNA-LNP vaccine designed to enhance mutation-specific immune responses. In vitro expression was confirmed in HeLa cells. In vivo immunization in mice induced strong interferon (IFN)-γ secretion, particularly against BRCA2 H143R, K801R, and T1425P mutations. Beagles immunized with cBR2-cocktail mRNA-LNPs exhibited increased IFN-γ production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells after repeated dosing, without significant hematological or biochemical abnormalities. Mutation-derived mRNA-LNP vaccines safely induced mutation-specific T-cell responses in vivo. Although anticancer efficacy was not assessed, we established a preclinical foundation for developing mutation-targeted mRNA immunotherapies for CMT and underscored the translational relevance of the canine model for human BRCA2/p53-related cancers.

description:
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for approximately 85% of all diagnoses. For patients with metastatic NSCLC lacking actionable driver mutations (e.g., EGFR, ALK), the standard first-line therapeutic strategy involves immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) or programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) axis, administered either as monotherapy or in combination with platinum-doublet chemotherapy. While these regimens have significantly improved overall survival (OS), a substantial proportion of patients fail to derive durable clinical benefit, and long-term survival rates for metastatic disease remain suboptimal, often due to host-related factors that impair the anti-tumor immune response.

A critical determinant of poor therapeutic outcomes in advanced NSCLC is cancer-associated cachexia (CAC), a multifactorial paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by systemic inflammation, negative protein-energy balance, and the involuntary loss of skeletal muscle mass (sarcopenia). Primary observational studies demonstrate that nutritional derangements closely associated with cachexia - such as significant weight loss and malnutrition - are highly prevalent in lung cancer, particularly in advanced disease, with lung cancer-specific cohorts reporting rates ranging from approximately 35% - 70% depending on disease stage and assessment method. Unlike starvation, it is driven by aberrant systemic inflammation and not fully reversible via nutritional support.

Clinically, cachexia is defined by the international consensus (Fearon criteria) as weight loss \>5% over 6 months, or weight loss \>2% in individuals with a body mass index (BMI) \< 20 kilograms per square meter (kg/m2) or sarcopenia. Sarcopenia is specifically defined by a low skeletal muscle index (SMI) at the L3 vertebral level, with widely validated cutoffs of \< 52.4 cm2/m2 for men and \< 8.5 cm2/m2 for women.

This is a Phase 1b/2, multi-site, single-arm, open-label, non-randomized study looking at whether adding tocilizumab to standard treatment for metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) is safe, possible, and effective. The study includes people with metastatic NSCLC, that is lung cancer that has spread, who have experienced significant loss of weight or muscle mass.

Primary Objective Evaluate the safety/feasibility and efficacy of adding tocilizumab to standard first-line chemo-immunotherapy in biomarker-selected patients with stage IV NSCLC, defined by weight loss ≥5% within the prior 6 months, or ≥2% if BMI \< 20 kilograms per square meter (kg/m2).

Co-primary endpoint 1: Safety/Feasibility Proportion of patients completing four cycles of chemo-IO + tocilizumab without grade ≥3 autoimmune or non-hematological treatment-related adverse events (TRAE). Feasibility will be defined as ≥80% completion; unacceptable toxicity as \>30% incidence of grade ≥3 serious AEs.

Co-primary endpoint 2: Progression-Free Survival Rate at 6 months Proportion of patients alive and progression-free at 6 months after starting therapy per RECIST v1.1, estimated by Kaplan-Meier and presented with a 95% CI.

Secondary Objectives Assess the effect of tocilizumab on body composition, inflammatory biomarkers, and treatment response.

Secondary Endpoints: change in weight/muscle mass (CT-based sarcopenia/Fearon index); Overall Response Rate (ORR); median Overall Survival Rate; and CRP levels from baseline to end of treatment.

Correlative Objectives Evaluate associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and baseline inflammatory biomarkers (CRP) as well as molecular biomarkers (KRAS, STK11) identified by next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumor tissue.

Exploratory Objectives Identify associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and longitudinal measurements of CRP, IL-6, Cyclin D1 and Bcl-xL mRNA, as well as baseline PTPRT methylation.

Participants will go through the screening and baseline process to assess eligibility. If eligible, participants will attend study treatment visits every 21 days for about 3 months, an End of Treatment (EOT) visit about 30 days after the last dose of treatment, and follow up for up to 12 months after the EOT visit. Tocilizumab will be administered in addition to standard treatment regimens for NSCLC, at a dose of 8 mg/kg intravenous (IV) once every three weeks (once every 21 days); on day one of each treatment cycle. Tocilizumab is administered as a single IV drip infusion over 1 hour; it cannot be administered as bolus or push. Tocilizumab will be given for 4 doses, at the beginning of treatment, or until disease progression or unacceptable toxicities.

The study will be open at 4 VA hospitals, and planned enrollment is about 43 participants in total with about 11 participants from each site. This research study is expected to take about 4 years. Individual participation in the study will take about 18 months.

abstract: RNA editing and splicing are two important post-transcriptional processing steps in plant chloroplasts. Evidence gathered in recent years indicates that these two steps are often tightly connected, although the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here, we elucidate that the splicing protein CFM2 is associated with the MORF2/MORF9 editors and is involved in editing-splicing coupling within plant chloroplasts. Using immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS) and in vitro/in vivo interaction assays, we identified the chloroplast splicing factor CFM2 as a direct physical interactor of the core editosome components MORF2 and MORF9. Disruption of CFM2 in Arabidopsis thaliana results in an albino-lethal phenotype, accompanied not only by impaired splicing of specific group II introns (e.g., ycf3.1, ndhA, and ndhB) but also by severe defects in RNA editing across multiple chloroplast sites, phenocopying morf2 and morf9 mutants. Conversely, mutations in the MORF genes analogously compromise splicing efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this mechanistic coupling is evolutionarily conserved between dicots and monocots, as loss of the rice homolog OsCFM2 drastically impairs site-specific editing. Together, our findings provide compelling evidence that, the MORF-CFM2 complex forms a physical association, coordinating the dual maturation of chloroplast transcripts to ensure photosynthetic function and plant viability.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) remain underexplored relative to siRNA and mRNA LNPs. Using an orthogonal workflow (DLS, NTA, AF4), we show that ionisable lipid identity and microfluidic flow rate govern key LNP attributes. Replacing SM-102 with MC3 increased size and reduced ASO recovery, while lower flow rates increased LNP size and improved recovery, highlighting formulation-property relationships for ASO LNP optimisation.

abstract: Live-cell nuclear imaging continues to be limited by the number of fluorescent moieties that may be recruited to the DNA locus of interest. Major advances in dCas9-based live-cell imaging have been made using plasmid-based expression systems that integrate many protein fluorophores into the dCas9 fluorescent ribonucleoprotein (fRNP) complex to increase the visibility of the resulting DNA labels. The dependence on exogenous DNA plasmids, however, precludes these strategies from applications where precise control of fRNP presence is necessary or possible plasmid integration into the genome is unacceptable. In this study, we evaluated the capacity for fluorescent guide RNA (gRNA) to improve the visibility of cellular DNA labels during live-cell imaging, bypassing the need for complex fluorescent protein expression and foreign DNA plasmid delivery. Both CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) components of the gRNA were modified with terminal cyanine 3 (Cy3) fluorophores before assembly into fRNP, and the impact on the brightness and signal-to-background (SNB) of the resulting DNA labels was evaluated at two different genomic loci: a repeat-rich Chr3 locus and chromosome telomeres. We further explored the visibility of DNA labeled with a "split" fRNP constructed from two individual tracrRNA fragments, rather than the complete 86 nt tracrRNA sequence, in order to reduce the costs and turnaround time of tracrRNA synthesis and to increase the terminal ends available for fluorophore modification. The 86 nt tracrRNA configuration bearing two terminal Cy3 modifications to both the crRNA and tracrRNA resulted in the greatest improvement to label visibility with a 190% increase in brightness and a 60% increase in SNB for both loci, on average, in comparison to the previously published fRNP containing only one Cy3 on the crRNA. The split tracrRNA fRNP was capable of labeling both genomic loci with varying success, imparting a maximum brightness improvement of 153% and an SNB improvement of 49% to Chr3 labeling, however, with no significant gains to brightness and 41% improved SNB for telomeres. For both the designs, label visibility improved consistently with additional fluorescence modification of the gRNA, indicating that the modifications were well tolerated, and further enhancement of gRNA fluorescence may continue to improve label visibility during live-cell imaging.

abstract: Delivering therapeutic mRNA relies on lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Finding optimal process parameters for new lipid combinations in LNP formulations remains a challenge. We used an automated, self-regulating microfluidic formulation platform developed for PEG-containing LNPs that actively changes process parameters to meet preset LNP diameters, and now explore how this automated production setup can be expanded to LNPs decorated with poly(2-oxazoline) (POx)-lipids. We also examine how the choice of lipopolymer affects the resulting physicochemical properties and in vivo biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. For that, we tested new LNPs by swapping poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) lipopolymers for alternatives based on poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline) (PMeOx) and poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx). For both POx-lipid variants, the platform independently identified optimal production conditions in four or fewer iterative cycles, yielding particles of the preset size and high mRNA encapsulation. Small-angle X-ray scattering revealed that smaller LNPs modified with PEtOx had greater structural surface variety and higher mRNA loading efficiency. When multiplexing these formulations in mice, the PEtOx-containing LNPs accumulated more in bone marrow and liver (and less in spleen and pancreas), compared to those with PEG, indicating trends that the chemistry of the lipopolymer affects the biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. By combining automated formulation and in vivo multiplexed testing, our approach provides a practical way to rapidly plan, formulate, and evaluate large pharmaceutical design spaces to select excipients and process parameters yielding optimal biological performance of LNPs.

abstract: To determine whether short-term pre-operative nivolumab either as monotherapy or in combination with low dose doxorubicin or novel IO combinations can induce immune activation in early BC.

institutions.label: Bristol-Myers Squibb

description: The investigators aim to test the activity of nivolumab monotherapy in primary breast tumors in a pre-operative window of opportunity trial. As the data of the investigators generated in the TONIC trial (metastatic TNBC) indicate that low dose doxorubicin may 'prime' the tumor microenvironment (TME) resulting in higher response rates on nivolumab, in addition, cohorts for treatment with nivolumab plus low dose doxorubicin will be opened. Given the emerging data on other immunomodulatory strategies, this platform study allows opening additional cohorts for promising novel immune-oncology (IO) drugs for which a strong efficacy signal has been seen without drug safety issues. The investigators will study the TME and systemic host factors with specific emphasis on immunosuppressive processes that can potentially be targeted by novel IO agents to further optimize BC immunotherapy.

abstract:
This study is researching an investigational drug, ALN-HSD called "study drug". This study is focused on participants who are known to have Metabolic dysfunction-Associated SteatoHepatitis (MASH). MASH is a form of Metabolic dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD). MASH occurs when fat builds up in liver cells, damaging them, and making the liver inflamed and stiff from fibrosis (scar tissue). MASH can progress to cirrhosis (long term scarring) and liver failure (when the liver cannot perform its job). The aim of the study is to see the effect of the study drug on lessening liver scarring related to MASH.

The study is looking at several other research questions, including:

* How ALN-HSD works to improve liver function and lessen MASH-related inflammation in the liver
* What side effects may happen from receiving the study drug
* How much study drug and study drug metabolites (byproduct of the body breaking down the study drug) are in the blood at different times
* Better understanding of the study drug and MASH

abstract:
This study will test a Regeneron study drug called ALN-CIDEB to find out whether it may help treat a liver disease called alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD). ALD is a type of liver disease caused by drinking alcohol at levels that are harmful to the body. The study will also test ALN-CIDEB in participants who are known to have metabolic dysfunction- and alcohol- associated liver disease (MetALD), a subgroup of people that have features of both ALD and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).

The study will compare 2 different dose regimens of ALN-CIDEB with placebo (something that looks like the study drug but doesn't contain any medicine) to understand how well ALN-CIDEB works to lower the amount of fat in the liver.

The study is looking at:

* What side effects ALN-CIDEB might cause
* How well ALN-CIDEB works to change liver fat and stiffness of the liver
* How ALN-CIDEB could affect the liver proteins

abstract: This phase 1 study will evaluate the safety, tolerability, and immune responses of two experimental mRNA HIV vaccines in adults living with HIV who are in overall good health. The study will enroll about 42 participants at multiple study sites. Researchers will assess whether these vaccines can start or strengthen antibody responses against HIV. The study will also evaluate how a closely monitored planned pause in antiretroviral therapy affects these immune responses.
